headline: Approved $200,000 from Housing Trust Fund for Dorset Commons; asked staff to review city power over building energy rules.
summary: Heard updates on regional planning, housing trends, and Town Meeting TV, which asked for $56,491 from the city. Postponed five agenda items and endorsed a joint housing needs study with the regional planning commission. The homeland security grant application passed 4-1 after one member raised concerns about possible federal conditions.
decisions: Postponed agenda items 12, 13, 14, 15, and 17 to future agendas, unanimously.
Approved consent agenda items a, c, and d, unanimously.
Approved applying for a FFY2026 State Homeland Security Grant, 4-1 with Dr. Zigmund opposed.
Approved $200,000 from the Housing Trust Fund for the Champlain Housing Trust Dorset Commons project, unanimously.
Endorsed issuing the joint housing needs and action plan request for quotes with the regional planning commission, unanimously.
Approved asking staff to review the city's authority over building energy rules, 3-2 with Mr. Barritt and Ms. Fitzgerald opposed.

PAGE 1 
DRAFT MINUTES 
 CITY COUNCIL 
     2 NOVEMBER 2026 
 
The South Burlington City Council held a regular meeting on Monday, 2 
November 2026, at 6:30 p.m., in the Auditorium, 180 Market Street, and by Zoom. 
 
MEMBERS PRESENT: T. Barritt, Chair; E. Fitzgerald, L. Smith, A. Chalnick, Dr. B. 
Zigmund 
 
ALSO PRESENT: J. Baker, City Manager; N. Storellicastro, Deputy City Manager; 
Chief C. Corbin, Fire Department; P. Conner, Director of Planning & Zoning; N. 
Senecal, H. Garcia, V. Bolduc, S. Dooley, C. Baker, C. Shaw, R. Doyle, J. Mitchell, 
A., D., and E. Treston, A. Allen, M. Tedder 
 
1. Pledge of Allegiance: 
 
The Pledge of Allegiance was recited. 
 
2. Instructions on exiting building in case of emergency and review of 
technology options: 
 
Ms. Baker provided instructions on emergency exit from the building and 
reviewed technology options. 
  
3. Additions, deletions or changes in the order of Agenda items: 
 
Ms. Baker asked to reverse the order of the two Executive Session items. 
 
Mr. Chalnick suggested postponing Items 12, 13, 14, 15, and 17 to a future agenda 
as several members of the Council had to be at the polls in the morning.  Mr. 
Chalnick also suggested a special meeting for Item 12.  Members agreed to start 
that discussion at the special meeting on Friday afternoon.
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 2 
Mr. Chalnick then moved to postpone Agenda items 12, 13, 14, 15, and 17 to 
future agendas.  Mr. Smith seconded.  Motion passed unanimously. 
 
4. Comments and questions from the public not related to the agenda: 
 
East Terrace residents asked about the next step in their ongoing traffic/parking 
issues.  Mr. Barritt noted that speed limit signs have been installed.  A resident 
said people don’t obey them, and the parking situation is getting worse.  Mr. 
Storellicastro said he has a package to bring to the Council’s 16 November 
meeting.   
 
5. Councilors Announcements and Reports on Committee Assignments                                                        
and City Manager’s Report: 
 
Council members reported on recent meetings and events they had attended. 
 
Ms. Baker:  Introduced the City’s new Economic Development Director Alex 
Armani-Munn. 
 
         Reminded voters that the polls open at 7 a.m. tomorrow. 
 
Fire Chief Corbin graduated from the National Fire Academy's 
Executive Fire Officer Program.  This multi-year program executive-level 
professionals with advanced skills in strategic management, public policy, 
community resilience, and long-term organizational planning. Chief Corbin 
becomes only the 15th Vermont fire professional to achieve this credential in the 
program's 40 year history.   
 
       There have been 181 responses to the FY28 budget survey. 
 
      The RFP is out for the Shelburne Road Center project. 
 
      The City has partnered with the Howard Center for the hiring of an 
Services Coordinator.  Chief Breault has been involved in that process. 
 
      The City’s Canine Officer has completed the Drug Certification program. 
 
      One lane on I-89 northbound will be closed on Wednesday morning.
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 3 
      The clarifier at the Airport Parkway Sewage Treatment Plant is near 
completion. 
 
      There will be night work on Williston Road prior to repaving next year. 
 
6. Consent Agenda: 
a. Consider and Sign Disbursements 
b. Approve the application for a FFY2026 State Homeland Security 
Grant to assist in funding the City’s Emergency Operations Plan 
c. Authorize the Director of Public Works to enter into plowing 
agreements for the 2026-2027 year for private roadways which 
have been dedicated to the City for future acceptance.  Further, 
authorize the Director of Public Works to enter into a wastewater 
maintenance agreement for the 2026-2027 year for the Spear 
Meadows neighborhood which has been dedicated to the City for 
future acceptance. 
d. Appoint Isaac Theodore Reicin to serve a 3-year term on the 
Development Review Board 
 
Dr. Zigmund asked to remove item 6b for discussion. 
 
Mr. Chalnick moved to approve Consent Agenda Items a, c, and d.  Ms. Fitzgerald 
seconded.  Motion passed unanimously. 
 
Dr. Zigmund said the Department of Homeland Security may not be good for 
residents of the City.  She was concerned that there could be “strings” attached to 
the grant including electronic scrutiny.  She said there have been instances where 
grants have been blocked because recipients didn’t comply with federal 
requirements.  Municipalities have been “bludgeoned” into election security 
requirements.  This is happening in multiple states.  She did not feel the City 
should tie itself to this. 
 
Ms. Baker said the City has applied for these funds in the past.   
 
Ms. Fitzgerald said she read through it and didn’t see anything like what Dr. 
Zigmund described.  She suggested approving it for this project with the 
understanding that there is a potential risk. 
 
Chief Corbin said there are no conditions, and this falls in line with the City’s 
Emergency Management Plan.
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 4 
 
Dr. Zigmund said the conditions happened after the grant money was awarded. 
 
Mr. Smith suggested applying.  If there are no strings, use the money; if there are 
strings, not accept the funds.    
 
Mr. Chalnick then moved to approve 6b.  Ms. Fitzgerald seconded.  Motion passed 
4-1 with Dr. Zigmund voting against. 
 
7. Receive and possibly approve a Housing Committee 
recommendation that $200,000 be allocated from the Housing Trust 
Fund to the Champlain Housing Trust Dorset Commons project : 
 
Members of the Housing Committee reviewed the history.  Ms. Senecal said the 
project is part of $25,000,000 improvements.  The project comprises 105 units 
across from the South Burlington Middle School which need to be upgraded for 
energy efficiency and more.  The work meets many elements of the City Plan and 
other city initiatives.  It will help keep this permanently affordable development. 
 
Ms. Fitzgerald added that it is also consistent with the goals of the Housing Trust. 
 
Mr. Smith moved to approve the $200,000 allocation from the Housing Trust Fund 
to the Champlain Housing Trust Dorset Commons project as presented.  Mr. 
Chalnick seconded.  
 
Ms. Fitzgerald noted this uses about 60% of the existing funds.  She suggested the 
funding mechanism may have to be revisited. 
 
Committee members noted that residents of 2 households have lived there for 30 
years, and residents of 11 households have lived there for more than 10 years.  
The hope is to keep it sustainable for the next 30 years. 
 
Mr. Barritt asked about the heating system.  Mr. Garcia said it is gas—fired Renais 
with backup electric resistance.  Phase 2 of the project will be to replace the 
Renais with heat pumps. 
 
In the vote that followed, the motion passed unanimously. 
 
8. Receive the Chittenden County Regional Planning Commission 
Annual Report:
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 5 
 
Mr. Baker shared his written report.  Ms. Baker said this is a great example of 
regional work which increases the City’s capacity to do a lot of planning. 
 
Mr. Baker outlined South Burlington projects in the Transportation Improvement 
Program (TIP), including: 
 
a. Airport Drive infiltration project 
b. Bartlett Bay culvert replacement 
c. Butler Farms culvert 
d. U.S. 2 improvements to Dorset Street 
e. Williston Road bridge and pedestrian improvements 
f. Williston Road sidewalk segments 
g. Hinesburg Road shared use path 
h. Expansion of Kennedy Drive stormwater pond #7 
 
Regional activities include the Chittenden County Brownfields Project and the 
Chittenden County Communications Union District. 
 
Transportation efforts include: 
 
a. Safety Action Plan 
b. Traffic Alert program 
c. Transportation Demand Management (TMD) 
d. Active transportation planning 
e. Older adults/people with disabilities transportation program 
f. Exit 14 scoping study 
 
A new area of activity is Partnership and Engagement which has included: 
 
a. Municipal elected official forums 
b. Legislative breakfasts 
c. Public Partnership Plan 
d. Community engagement data base 
e. Municipal Equity Community Practice 
 
The Unified Planning Work Program has included: 
 
a. UPWP web page 
b. Transportation scoping
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 6 
c. Outreach/engagement assistance 
d. Technical assistance (e.g., GIS, traffic counts, pavement condition 
assessments) 
 
9. Hold a Council requested conversation on housing trends and 
targets in the State, County, and City: 
 
Mr. Baker began by explaining the difference between a “forecast” and a “target.”  
A forecast is a likely future condition based on existing trends while a target is a 
goal for new housing required by the Legislature.  He then said that trend forecast 
details aim to develop a forecast suitable for transportation and regional planning 
for the Agency of Transportation (AOT) and CCRPC.  Mr. Baker said the State has 
no official long-term forecast for population. 
 
Mr. Baker said some forecasts are optimistic showing a slow, stable growth with a 
return of international and domestic migration to reduce population decline. 
 
Dr. Zigmund asked what data they are looking at.  Mr. Baker said when you do 
long-range forecasting, you don’t go lineally.  It is a bad time for migration, but 
that doesn’t mean it will be permanent.   
 
Mr. Baker then showed a chart of Draft Comparisons of Projections of Population 
by county with Chittenden County showing a population growth of 14,000 from 
168,412 to 182,000.  He also showed Draft Housing Forecasts and noted the 
decline in household size.  This means more units are needed to house the same 
number of people.  There are now 2.3 people per household.  By 2050, that 
number will be reduce to 2 people per household. 
 
Mr. Baker also showed a graph of Employment Forecasts.  Chittenden County is 
still expected to be an economic driver with a third of jobs in the state being 
located there. 
 
With regard to housing targets, Mr. Baker showed a chart of Vermont Housing 
Needs Assessment which indicates a deficit of 7000 units.  He said that the 
purpose of setting housing target goals is to replace lost/seasonal homes.  He 
stressed that there are no punitive consequences for not meeting the targets. 
 
Mr. Conner said the effort to assign those units locally was a regional effort.  It 
provides an opportunity to quantitatively assess how we are doing.  Mr. Baker
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 7 
said the State is trying to put objective numbers instead of just saying “more.”  
He then reviewed lower, medium and upper range targets. 
 
Mr. Smith said he did not see how population growth and housing target growth 
square up.   
 
Dr. Zigmund said more homes have been built, but there are more homeless than 
ever before because those homeless cannot afford what is being built.  She would 
like to see more evidence that the homeless are being helped by building more 
units. 
 
Mr. Baker said there are a bunch of different dynamics.  New homes are not being 
built for the lowest element of the market.  A person moving into the larger 
housing unit probably moved out of the next one lower down on the scale, etc.     
The vacancy rates are not healthy.  
 
Ms. Baker clarified that the goal was not just to build homes, it was to address 
workforce and social needs gaps in the State.  
 
Ms. Fitzgerald said the low to middle range of targets is consistent with what 
South Burlington’s growth has been, but there are other stakeholder groups that 
are not being served (e.g., seniors, disabled, special needs). 
 
Mr. Baker said they crafted the middle target that was more reasonable, but he 
noted that the trend is similar to the low-end target.  He felt that trend is where 
we’re heading without policy intervention.  He stressed that this is not growth for 
growth’s sake. 
 
Mr. Baker then outlined issues to address including: 
 
a. Land use and housing 
b. Climate mitigation 
c. Climate adaptation 
d. Transportation safety 
e. Open space 
 
He said targets are used to develop scenarios, to meet the policy goals and 
evaluate the planned investments and policies to best balance all of the goals of 
residents and make progress in the most sustainable way possible.
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 8 
Mr. Conner said it is a question of where we put our resources locally, regionally, 
statewide, etc.  Mr. Smith said the how and where are very important. 
 
Ms. Senecal said when talking about “homes,” this can also be apartments, 
condos, townhouses, etc.  That also informs what kind of housing is needed. 
 
Mr. Baker then outlined the next steps: 
 
a. Regional Housing Assessment 
b. Report/materials on the role/purpose of CCRPC 
c. Municipal Housing Action Plan 
 
He noted that the Legislature is requiring someone to track housing in the State.  
Dr. Zigmund asked if this includes second homes as there are several on her 
street.  Mr. Baker said it is much harder when you get down to occupancy. 
 
Mr. Doyle said that though there are no punitive consequences, there are real 
consequences for the people who can’t get housing.  He spoke of people who 
have had to move out of the area and commute an hour to their jobs and be away 
from older parents who need their assistance. 
 
Mr. Baker ended by thanking South Burlington for all it is doing. 
 
10. Receive an update, as set forth in the FY27 Policy Priorities and 
Strategies, on a collaboration with CCRPC on a shared Housing 
Needs Assessment and Housing Action Plan Pilot and potentially 
endorse this approach: 
 
Mr. Conner said everything they have been talking about is a single number.  The 
City is “off-kilter” to be a healthy demographic community.  The CCRPC RFQ will 
address what levers the City can pull to address this.  He asked whether the 
Council would accept this approach. 
 
Mr. Barritt asked if this has been done before in Vermont.  Mr. Conner said 
housing needs studies end quickly in a number; they don’t go to what is needed to 
be a “community.”  There may be tools outside of what has been done in the 
past, and this does not necessarily mean houses.  He also noted that what the City 
learns can be shared with other communities. 
 
Dr. Zigmund suggested the need for a more accurate estimate of the vacancy rate.
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 9 
Mr. Baker said there is a consultant who does look at vacancy rates. 
 
Mr. Conner said this would be largely on the regional level but would touch on 
things the Council has been talking about.   
 
Mr. Baker said Chittenden County has a lower number of second homes 
compared to other places in the state.  They are mainly used as B&Bs. 
 
Ms. Baker noted that the State was looking at how to change the classification of 
properties to better report on the State-wide grand list.    
 
Mr. Smith said one important step to take relates to the aging population who are 
living in 3-4 bedroom homes that would be ideal for a family.  He felt these people 
should be encouraged to move.  He asked if more homes would be needed if 
senior homes were created. 
 
It was noted that one recent challenge is that downtown living is mostly 1 or 2 
bedroom units, not appropriate for a family.  And most are apartments/rentals.  
 
Mr. Chalnick cited the need to focus on ownership so people can build equity.  He 
said he was uncomfortable with the 3rd bullet point regarding meeting the housing 
targets.  He was OK with the low target, but he didn’t feel the City should be 
shooting for the high target.  Mr. Conner stressed that the City’s action plan is 
implementing the City Plan. 
 
Ms. Dooley noted that at a Housing Committee Meeting, Ms. Peterson gave 
members a document regarding a study relative to low and middle housing. 
 
Dr. Zigmund then moved to endorse the issuance of the joint RFQ with CCRPC as 
presented.  Mr. Smith seconded.   
 
Mr. Conner noted that another vote will be needed for funding of this effort.  Mr. 
Baker added that the scope of the study can be regulated to address what the City 
wants, and they can figure out the cost. 
 
In the vote that followed, the motion passed unanimously. 
 
11. Receive the Town Meeting TV Annual Report and Budget 
presentation:
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 10 
Ms. Mitchell provided a background of Town Meeting TV.  She noted that last year 
they produced 1,712 programs, 370 of which were municipal.  They currently do 5 
meetings and one other program a month for South Burlington.  Last year, they 
did a total of 89 meetings for the City.  They also go out into the community, and 
recently did the grand opening of the City Center Park. 
 
Ms. Mitchell then explained their funding through cable TV subscribers and local 
municipalities.  This year’s request from South Burlington is $56,491, a 5% 
increase over last year.  $26,802 of that amount is for municipal meetings.  Ms. 
Mitchell also explained their other funding sources. 
 
Ms. Tedder said they are very responsive to any program the City wants to cover.  
She suggested possibly doing something with the new Economic Development 
person.  She also recognized the Superintendent of Schools continuing program 
“In the Know with Dr. Joe.” 
 
A new website was launched in October.  Viewers can get right to South 
Burlington, and there is a button for each of the municipal meetings. 
 
When asked about AI, Ms. Mitchell said they will be very cautious about bringing 
it in so that nothing goes out that hasn’t first been viewed by human eyes. 
 
Ms. Baker praised the diligent and dependable work of Town Meeting TV’s Travis 
Washington in recording meetings. 
 
Mr. Smith said the 5% increase is more than the City is looking at.  Ms. Mitchell 
said this is what they are asking of everyone, but they are very willing to sit down 
and discuss it with staff.  Ms. Tedder stressed that this is not a cost of living 
increase; it is to address the decrease from cable subscriber revenue.  This year, 
they lost 10% from Comcast.  Ms. Tedder also asked the City to support them 
when they go to the Legislature to ask for support with some issues. 
 
12. Postponed. 
13. Postponed. 
14. Postponed. 
15. Postponed 
 
16. Discuss an intended legal opinion on municipal authority to regulate 
building and thermal energy systems:
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 11 
Ms. Baker requested that the Council be as specific as possible. 
 
Mr. Chalnick said he wants to know what authority the City has and has not to 
implement climate change regulations including what buildings they can cover.  
Mr. Smith added that as a Dillon Rule state, how the City can get authority it does 
not have. 
 
Ms. Fitzgerald said she is looking for balance and said she sensed that many of 
the things on Mr. Chalnick’s list are government overreach and incremental costs.  
She said she would not support everything on the list. 
 
Dr. Zigmund said they are just trying to ask what authority the City has and what 
might be possible.  Mr. Smith added that if they get answers, they may not do 
anything.  He just wanted to see a menu of options.  Dr. Zigmund said if they get 
an answer to what is possible, they can act more quickly on a thermal plan.  She 
felt the cost of doing nothing is greater than doing something now.  She felt it 
would also save money down the road.  Not doing something now shifts the crisis 
to our children and grandchildren. 
 
Mr. Barritt cited the need to be specific about what Mr. Chalnick wants to do in the 
future (e.g., tell people they can’t replace a gas burner with a gas burner?)  Mr. 
Chalnick read his list of items as follows: 
• We need to understand what authority we have to implement climate 
change policy with respect to existing buildings.  I anticipate that the 
thermal implementation plan may have items similar to the following: 
o Require carbon emission and energy efficiency scores for buildings 
o Require energy audits and possibly require implementation of 
recommendations that are cost effective 
o Require contractors to provide carbon-free alternatives 
o Required time of sale residential/time of listing rental carbon 
emission and efficiency scores 
o Achieve building emission standards that become more stringent 
over time 
o Require replacement of end-of -life fossil fuel equipment with carbon-
efficient systems where technology allows and economically feasible 
 
Ms. Fitzgerald said she feels the items on this list will cause rents to go up.  South 
Burlington is not an affordable community now.  She also saw administrative 
costs.  She stressed that “authority grabs” are not very welcome in communities.  
She asked to wait for the plan and then react to it.
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 12 
 
Mr. Smith said that unless looking into this will be very expensive and onerous to 
staff, he felt it would be very helpful.  He also said that efficient homes are more 
affordable.  Mr. Barritt disagreed and said this would make it harder for people to 
afford their homes. 
 
Dr. Zigmund said that historically fossil fuel prices have been volatile while the 
cost of renewable energy has been dropping.  She also cited other potential 
health costs from fossil fuels.  She felt this was an exploratory exercise and didn’t 
necessarily mean they would go down this road. 
 
Ms. Baker said the cost could range between $5,000 and $10,000.  She noted there 
is a budget for outside legal work which would cover this. 
 
Mr. Smith then moved to ask staff to review what Mr. Chalnick has put forward to 
see where the City’s authority lies.  Mr. Chalnick seconded.  The motion passed 3-
2 with Mr. Barritt and Ms. Fitzgerald voting against. 
 
17. Postponed. 
 
18. Review the significant agenda topics for the Council’s 10 November 
Council Meeting: 
 
a. Receive an Actuarial update on the South Burlington Pension 
Program 
b. Receive a presentation from the Library Board of Trustees on 
their 5-year Strategic Plan 
c. Approve a Legislative Advocacy Agenda for the 2027-2028 
Biennium 
d. Consider approving a resolution to increase fees for parking 
tickets and creating a Parking Fund 
e. Items postponed from tonight’s agenda 
 
19. Other Business: 
 
No other business was presented. 
 
20. Consider entering into executive session pursuant to 1 V.S.A. 
Section 313(a)(1)(F) and (2) for the purpose of receiving confidential 
attorney-client communications and discussing the negotiation of
CITY COUNCIL 2 November 2026 PAGE 13 
real estate lease or purchase options, specifically the Williston Road 
Pump Station: and 
21. Consider entering into executive session pursuant to 1 V.S.A. 
Section 313(a)(1)(F) and (2) for the purpose of receiving confidential 
attorney-client communications and discussing the negotiation of 
real estate lease or purchase options, specifically 1720 Spear Street: 
 
Ms. Fitzgerald move that the Council make a specific finding that premature 
general public knowledge of the Council’s receipt of confidential attorney-client 
communications and discussion of the negotiating or securing of real estate 
purchase or lease options regarding: 
a. Williston Road Pump Station and 
b. 1720 Spear Street 
clearly place this public body at a substantial disadvantage.  Mr. Smith seconded 
the motion when then passed unanimously. 
 
Ms. Fitzgerald then moved that the City Council enter into executive session under 
1 V.S.A. Section 313(a)(1)(F) and (2) for the purpose of receiving confidential 
attorney-client communications and discussing the negotiating or securing of real 
estate purchase or lease options regarding: 
a. Williston Road Pump Station and 
b. 1720 Spear Street 
inviting into the session Ms. Baker, Mr. Storellicastro, Mr. Conner and Mr. McNeil 
and noting that Mr. Chalnick will be recused from the 1720 Spear Street session 
due to a potential conflict of interest.  Mr. Smith seconded.  The motion then 
passed unanimously.   
 
Mr. Chalnick left executive session after the discussion of the Williston Road 
Pump Station at approximately 10:00 pm.   
 
At 10:15 pm Mr. Smith moved to exit executive session.  Ms. Fitzgerald seconded.  
The motion passed 4-0. 
 
As there was no further business to come before the Council, Mr. Smith moved 
to adjourn.  Ms. Fitzgerald seconded.  Motion passed unanimously.  The meeting 
was adjourned at 10:16 p.m.
